passage:
I'm Farhan. When Trisha's father died, I did not know what to say, so I made a pot of khichdi and rang the doorbell at the funeral house. I did not give advice. I sat on the floor with Trisha for two hours, sometimes talking about the old cricket matches, sometimes silent. Trisha cried once. I passed the tissues.
Two weeks later, when the visitors had stopped, I sent a message: "Walking past your lane, want a chai?" Then again after a month. It was small, and I felt awkward. But Trisha told me later that those messages were what got through the weeks when the house went quiet.

qa.q: What food did Farhan bring to the funeral house?
qa.a: Farhan brought khichdi.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when arriving at the door without knowing what to say?
qa.a: Farhan felt unsure and awkward, with no advice to give. Bringing food and sitting quietly was a way to help anyway.

qa.q: What small contact after the funeral turned out to matter most?
qa.a: Farhan sent short messages after two weeks and again after a month, asking about chai. They arrived when the visitors had stopped and the house went quiet.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Trisha when the visitors stopped?
qa.a: The house probably felt very quiet and lonely, since the crowd had gone. Farhan's small messages showed Trisha was still remembered.

grounding: A young adult brings food, sits at the funeral house without fixing anything, and keeps up small contact in the weeks after.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Friday. Dev's mother died last week, and Dev returned to the hostel yesterday. Pranav, a second-year in the next room, was the only one I saw do something useful. Pranav did not ask, "How are you?" or give advice. Pranav took two cups of tea to the terrace, sat next to Dev and said, "I'm here if you want to talk. Or not." They sat for an hour, mostly quiet.
This morning I noticed Pranav slipping a note under Dev's door: "Dinner at 8? I'll knock." Later I learned Pranav has been doing this every couple of days since.
Lakshmi, warden

qa.q: Where did Pranav take the two cups of tea?
qa.a: Pranav took the two cups of tea to the terrace.

qa.q: What might Pranav have wanted by saying "I'm here if you want to talk. Or not."?
qa.a: Pranav wanted Dev to feel supported without pressure, showing care and patience. Offering both choices leaves the decision to Dev.

qa.q: What did Pranav do in the following days that mattered?
qa.a: Pranav kept slipping notes under Dev's door, such as "Dinner at 8? I'll knock." Regular small contact counts when others fade.

qa.q: How might Dev have seen the note offering dinner?
qa.a: Dev may have seen it as a low-pressure sign that someone cared, since it asked for nothing but a meal. Pranav kept knocking even after the first days.

grounding: A young adult sits with a bereaved hostel mate on a terrace without fixing and keeps up small regular contact afterwards, noted by a warden.

passage:
Wednesday
Three weeks since Nusrat's father died. Today I went again after class, with a steel box of Ammi's khichdi.
On the funeral day the house was so full you couldn't sit. Everyone brought food and advice. Now it's quiet. Her aunt told me I'm the only friend still coming.
We sat on her bed. For the first half hour she didn't say anything, and I didn't push. I folded the clothes on the chair. Then she started talking about how her father used to hum while shaving, and she cried, and I just listened.
When I left she said, "Come Saturday?"
I will. I don't know how to fix any of this. I don't think I'm supposed to.
Salma

qa.q: What did Salma bring to Nusrat's house?
qa.a: Salma brought a steel box of Ammi's khichdi.

qa.q: What might Salma have been feeling while Nusrat stayed silent?
qa.a: Salma likely felt unsure and helpless but patient, choosing not to push and to simply stay.

qa.q: Which of Salma's choices mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Coming back regularly in the quiet weeks after, when others had faded, and letting Nusrat talk or stay silent.

qa.q: What do Salma's visits mean to Nusrat now?
qa.a: Nusrat feels less alone in the quiet house and wants the company, which is why she asks Salma to come on Saturday 🤍

grounding: A young adult brings food, sits with the bereaved and keeps coming in the weeks after, when others have faded.

passage:
Payal: hi. no need to reply. just saying I'm thinking of you and your mum today
Sarika: thanks
Payal: I'm going to the market Thursday. want me to drop some fruit and sit for a bit? we don't have to talk
Sarika: ok
[Thursday]
Payal: outside
Sarika: door's open
[later that night]
Sarika: thanks for today. you're the only one who still comes
Sarika: everyone came for the first four days and then it's like it never happened
Payal: I'll keep coming. Thursdays?
Sarika: Thursdays
Sarika: I liked that you didn't try to make me feel better
Payal: I don't know how to. I just know how to bring fruit

qa.q: When did Payal offer to drop some fruit?
qa.a: Payal offered to come on Thursday.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling about the people who stopped coming?
qa.a: Sarika felt lonely and hurt that everyone came for four days and then acted as though it never happened.

qa.q: Which of Payal's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Payal made small, regular contact, offered practical help and company without pressure to talk, and didn't try to fix the grief.

qa.q: What would change if Payal had stopped coming like the others?
qa.a: Sarika would likely feel even more alone, with no one marking the loss after the first few days.

grounding: A young adult keeps small, regular contact with a grieving friend, bringing food and sitting without fixing, after others fade.

passage:
The day Sudha's mother died, Gopika came before sunrise with a big pot of rice and dal, because she knew no fire would be lit in that village house. She said nothing much. She swept the courtyard and sat at the edge of the mat while women wept inside.
Sudha sat numb. Gopika didn't tell her to be strong. She just stayed, filling water pots, handing her a glass now and then.
The relatives left after the thirteenth day. The house fell silent.
Gopika kept coming. Every evening she walked over with something small: a few guavas, a tiffin, the newspaper. Some days Sudha talked about her mother's songs; some days she said nothing at all, and they shelled peas together.
A month later Sudha said, "When everyone left, you didn't." Gopika only nodded and passed her the next pod.

qa.q: What did Gopika bring before sunrise?
qa.a: Gopika brought a big pot of rice and dal.

qa.q: Why might Gopika have swept and filled water pots instead of talking?
qa.a: Gopika felt sad and protective towards Sudha and sensed words could not help, so she showed her care quietly through practical tasks.

qa.q: What made Gopika's support so valuable?
qa.a: She did practical things, let Sudha talk or stay silent, and kept coming every evening after the relatives left.

qa.q: How does Sudha see Gopika now?
qa.a: Sudha feels deeply grateful and comforted, noticing that when everyone else left, Gopika stayed.

grounding: A young adult brings food, sits at the house of mourning and keeps coming after others fade, letting the bereaved talk or be silent.

passage: The house in Kilimani, Nairobi, was full of relatives and plastic chairs the day after Lindiwe's mother died. Wanjiru arrived with a pot of githeri and made no speech. She put the pot in the kitchen, found a chair near Lindiwe, and sat. Some hours Lindiwe talked about her mother's terrible singing in the car; some hours she said nothing, and Wanjiru said nothing too, passing tea. After the funeral the chairs were returned and the visitors thinned out. Wanjiru didn't. Every Thursday she texted one line: "Thinking of you. Chapati at the canteen?" Most weeks Lindiwe came. Once she wrote back only, "Not today." Wanjiru replied, "Okay. Next Thursday." Six weeks in, over chapati, Lindiwe said quietly, "Everyone else stopped asking. You didn't."

qa.q: What did Wanjiru bring to the house?
qa.a: A pot of githeri.

qa.q: Why did Wanjiru reply "Okay. Next Thursday." when Lindiwe said "Not today"?
qa.a: Wanjiru was patient and caring, wanting Lindiwe to feel no pressure while still knowing someone would keep showing up.

qa.q: Which of Wanjiru's actions mattered most, and why?
qa.a: The steady weekly contact after the visitors thinned out, because that is when Lindiwe noticed everyone else had stopped asking.

qa.q: What was it like for Lindiwe six weeks in?
qa.a: Lindiwe felt that others had faded away, and Wanjiru's steady Thursday messages made her feel remembered.

grounding: Shows a young adult bringing food, sitting quietly at the house of mourning and keeping small, regular contact in the weeks after, when others fade.
